title: Binary Search
html:
Binary Search

Halving the search space each step: O(log n). Easy to state, easy to write subtly wrong, and applicable far beyond sorted arrays.

The invariant is the whole thing

Every correct binary search maintains one: the answer, if it exists, lies within [low, high]. Bugs come from updating the bounds in a way that breaks it, or from a loop that lets the range stop shrinking.

Two habits prevent most of them:

  • Compute the midpoint as low + (high - low) / 2. The naive sum overflows at large indices.
  • Decide what the loop guarantees on exit before writing it, then hand-check the empty and single-element cases.

Finding a boundary, not a value

Most real uses are not "find x" but "find the first position where a predicate becomes true" - lower bound, upper bound, insertion point, first failing version.

That needs the predicate to be monotonic over the range: false then true, never alternating. Given that, binary search applies whether or not the data is sorted in the ordinary sense. This is the insight worth carrying: it searches over decisions, not only over arrays.

Binary search on the answer

When a value is hard to compute but easy to check, search the answer space.

"What is the smallest capacity that finishes in d days" is hard head-on. "Given capacity c, does it finish in d days" is a simple simulation, and it is monotonic - more capacity never needs more days. So search the capacity between its sensible bounds. Cost becomes O(log(range) x cost of one check).

Rotated input

A rotated sorted array is still O(log n): one half is always properly sorted, and comparing the midpoint with an endpoint says which. Then decide which half can contain the target.

Duplicates break the guarantee - when the midpoint equals both ends you cannot tell which half is sorted, and the worst case degrades to O(n).

Common mistakes

  • An infinite loop from low = mid instead of mid + 1. If the range can fail to shrink, it will not terminate.
  • The wrong comparison in the loop condition, missing the single-element case.
  • Assuming sortedness the caller never promised.
  • Searching a predicate that is not really monotonic, and getting an answer that happens to be right on the sample.
